definition: The principle that relevantly similar individuals should receive similar treatment.
example: Check consistency for comparable cases.
caveat: Defining relevant similarity is itself a substantive choice.

definition: An attention-head behavior associated with continuing patterns by matching a repeated context and copying its successor.
example: Analyze in-context sequence repetition.
caveat: The canonical mechanism does not explain every form of in-context learning.

definition: Assumptions that make some solutions easier or more likely for a learner.
example: Convolutions favor local, shared image patterns.
caveat: Bias here does not necessarily mean unfairness.

definition: Using a model to produce outputs without its usual training update.
example: Generate tokens from a trained language model.
caveat: Statistical inference has a broader, different meaning.

definition: An interface that accepts inputs and returns model predictions or generated outputs.
example: Call a hosted classification service.
caveat: Endpoint behavior includes preprocessing and configuration, not just weights.

definition: Generating content that fits a gap while conditioning on surrounding material.
example: Fill a missing paragraph or code block.
caveat: Not all infilling models use the same training objective.

definition: A contrastive classification objective selecting a positive pair among negative alternatives.
example: Train paired-view or image-text representations.
caveat: Its mutual-information interpretation relies on assumptions.

definition: The decrease in entropy or another specified uncertainty measure after conditioning or splitting.
example: Choose a tree split that reduces label uncertainty.
caveat: Specify the uncertainty measure and normalization.

definition: Finding relevant items from a collection for an information need.
example: Retrieve documents matching a query.
caveat: Relevance differs from factual correctness.

definition: The problem of whether learned objectives or internal optimization, when present, match the training objective.
example: Study whether a learned optimizer pursues the intended objective out of distribution.
caveat: Not every trained model is established to contain a distinct inner optimizer.

definition: Filling or replacing selected missing regions of an image or other structured input.
example: Restore a masked portion of an image.
caveat: A plausible reconstruction is not evidence of the original content.

definition: The stage receiving the model's initial input representation.
example: Read a vector of normalized features.
caveat: An input interface may have no trainable parameters.

definition: Normalizing each example and channel over spatial positions.
example: Use normalization in image-style transfer.
caveat: It can remove information useful for some recognition tasks.

definition: Predicting a separate pixel mask for each individual object instance.
example: Separate the silhouettes of three overlapping people.
caveat: Instance identifiers are distinct from semantic class labels.

definition: A prioritization scheme for resolving conflicts among instruction sources.
example: Distinguish application policy from quoted document instructions.
caveat: The hierarchy must be supported by training and system controls.

definition: Training on tasks expressed as instructions paired with desired responses.
example: Improve a model's ability to follow varied requests.
caveat: Instruction following is not the same as reliable reasoning.

definition: A model adapted to respond to instructions rather than only continue arbitrary text.
example: Use a chat-oriented checkpoint.
caveat: The expected prompt format remains model-specific.

definition: The hypothesis that many different goals can favor similar intermediate strategies, such as retaining resources.
example: Analyze incentives for preserving future action options.
caveat: It is conditional on goals, capabilities, and environment assumptions.

definition: An attribution method integrating input gradients along a path from a baseline to the input.
example: Attribute an image classifier's score to pixels.
caveat: Baseline and path choices influence interpretation.

definition: A measure of how consistently different annotators label the same data.
example: Measure agreement on a sentiment annotation batch.
caveat: Agreement is not the same as correctness.

definition: The elapsed time between successive generated output tokens, or an average of that interval.
example: Measure smoothness of streamed responses.
caveat: Averages can hide stalls and long-tail delays.

definition: A feature representing joint dependence on two or more inputs.
example: Multiply price by promotion status.
caveat: Interactions may be missed by purely additive models.

definition: How well a study supports the claimed explanation within its tested setting.
example: Control confounders when comparing training methods.
caveat: Internal validity does not guarantee broad generalization.

definition: Estimating values between known observations or representations.
example: Resize an image or blend latent points.
caveat: Interpolating smoothly does not guarantee semantic validity.

definition: The regime where a model becomes able to fit the training data essentially exactly.
example: Study the peak in a double-descent curve.
caveat: The threshold depends on data, objective, and architecture.

definition: The extent or process by which a model's behavior or mechanisms can be understood under a specified standard.
example: Explain why a model makes a class prediction.
caveat: Interpretability has several non-equivalent definitions.

definition: Intersection size divided by union size for two sets or regions.
example: Compare a predicted box or mask with a reference.
caveat: Empty-set conventions and matching rules must be specified.

definition: A matrix that reverses an invertible linear transformation.
example: Solve a small nonsingular linear system.
caveat: Explicit inversion is often less stable than solving directly.

definition: Inferring a reward or preference model from observed behavior.
example: Infer objectives explaining expert demonstrations.
caveat: Many rewards can explain the same behavior.

definition: A vector-search structure partitioning vectors into coarse clusters and searching selected partitions.
example: Reduce comparisons in a large vector collection.
caveat: Searching too few partitions can miss relevant neighbors.

definition: A structure mapping terms to documents or positions where they occur.
example: Search a large text corpus efficiently.
caveat: It supports lexical matching rather than semantic understanding by itself.

definition: A neural network whose mapping can be reversed, subject to its defined input and output spaces.
example: Build an exact-likelihood flow model.
caveat: Invertibility alone does not imply a tractable Jacobian determinant.

definition: An anomaly detector based on how quickly random partitions isolate observations.
example: Flag unusual tabular records.
caveat: Rare but legitimate subgroups may be flagged.

definition: A manifold method preserving estimated geodesic distances on a neighborhood graph.
example: Unroll a curved low-dimensional data surface.
caveat: Poor graph connectivity can distort results.

definition: Fitting a monotonic function without imposing a fixed parametric shape.
example: Calibrate probabilities with a monotonic mapping.
caveat: It can overfit when calibration data is limited.

definition: The matrix of first derivatives of vector outputs with respect to vector inputs.
example: Analyze how outputs change with inputs.
caveat: A full Jacobian can be expensive to materialize.

definition: The product of a function's Jacobian with a chosen input-direction vector.
example: Measure output change along a parameter direction.
caveat: It avoids forming the full Jacobian.

definition: An input or intervention intended to bypass a model's behavioral restrictions.
example: Evaluate whether a safety boundary can be circumvented.
caveat: Jailbreak and prompt injection overlap but are not identical concepts.

definition: A symmetric, finite mixture-based divergence between probability distributions.
example: Compare two models' output distributions.
caveat: The divergence itself is not generally the metric; its square root is.

definition: A probability describing multiple events or variables together.
example: Model both a label and its input features.
caveat: A joint model is not automatically a causal model.

definition: Splitting data into k folds and using each fold once for validation.
example: Average validation scores across five fits.
caveat: Correlated observations require appropriate grouping.

definition: Clustering by alternating point-to-center assignments and centroid updates to reduce squared distances.
example: Group embeddings into k clusters.
caveat: It favors roughly spherical, similarly scaled clusters.

definition: A randomized initialization choosing spread-out starting centers for k-means.
example: Improve typical k-means convergence.
caveat: It improves initialization, not the general suitability of k-means.

definition: Clustering around selected observed representatives rather than mean vectors.
example: Cluster data with a non-Euclidean distance.
caveat: Results depend strongly on the chosen dissimilarity.

definition: Predicting from the labels or values of the k most similar stored examples.
example: Classify a point from neighboring feature vectors.
caveat: Feature scaling and distance choice strongly affect results.

definition: A space-partitioning tree for efficient geometric search in favorable dimensions.
example: Accelerate low-dimensional nearest-neighbor queries.
caveat: Performance often degrades in high dimensions.

definition: A similarity function that, when positive semidefinite, can represent inner products in a feature space.
example: Use an RBF kernel for nonlinear classification.
caveat: Not every arbitrary similarity is a valid PSD kernel.

definition: Using explicit finite features to approximate a kernel.
example: Scale kernel-like learning to larger datasets.
caveat: Approximation quality trades off against feature count.

definition: Estimating a density by smoothing contributions around observed points.
example: Estimate a one-dimensional score distribution.
caveat: Bandwidth often matters more than kernel shape.

definition: Combining multiple operations into fewer kernels to reduce launches and intermediate memory traffic.
example: Fuse elementwise operations around a matrix multiplication.
caveat: Fusion benefits depend on hardware and operation structure.
